questions.question: Two lizard species live on the same rocky outcrop (same habitat) without excluding each other. How is that possible in terms of niche?
questions.solution: Habitat is the ADDRESS; niche is the PROFESSION — the full set of resources used, times of activity, temperatures tolerated, food sizes taken. Two species sharing a habitat can partition it into different micro-niches (one hunts at dawn on boulders, the other at dusk in crevices), avoiding direct competition. Resource partitioning, not exclusion, is the resolution.

questions.question: Why do desert lizards bask in the morning and retreat to burrows at noon, while a polar bear's problem is quite different?
questions.solution: The lizard is an ectotherm — it must BEHAVIOURALLY move between heat sources and sinks to keep its body temperature functional (bask to warm, burrow/shade to cool). The polar bear is an endotherm generating its own heat; its problem in the Arctic is LOSING heat, solved by insulation (fur, blubber) and small extremities. Behavioural thermoregulation vs structural insulation.

questions.question: Why does a J-shaped growth curve eventually become impossible for any real population? Define carrying capacity and link it to the sigmoid curve.
questions.solution: Exponential growth dN/dt = rN assumes unlimited resources; in reality resources (food, space, mates) are finite. Carrying capacity K is the population size the environment can sustain; as N approaches K, resource limitation raises mortality/lowers births, bending the curve into a SIGMOID (logistic) form. The J is the early phase, not the destiny.

questions.question: A dandelion produces thousands of tiny seeds; an elephant produces one calf in years. Explain the two life-history strategies this contrast represents.
questions.solution: r-selected: many cheap offspring, no parental care, rapid reproduction in unstable environments — winning by QUANTITY (survival is a lottery). K-selected: few, expensive, cared-for offspring in stable near-capacity environments — winning by QUALITY and competitive ability. Neither is 'better'; each fits a different regime of disturbance and crowding.

questions.question: Classify these as +/−/0 interactions and give the key distinction: lichen, cuckoo-crow, cattle egret-grazing cattle, tapeworm-human, orchid on mango.
questions.solution: Lichen: MUTUALISM (+/+) — alga provides food, fungus provides minerals/shelter. Cuckoo-crow: BROOD PARASITISM (+/−) — cuckoo benefits, host loses. Cattle egret-grazing cattle: COMMENSALISM (+/0) — egret feeds on insects flushed by cattle, cattle unaffected. Tapeworm-human: PARASITISM (+/−) — parasite benefits, host harmed. Orchid on mango: COMMENSALISM (+/0) — orchid gets support, mango unharmed. The sign pattern is the classifier.

questions.question: Desert plants have thick cuticles, CAM photosynthesis and spines instead of leaves. Tie each feature to the specific problem it solves.
questions.solution: Thick cuticle/sunken stomata: cut water LOSS (transpiration). CAM: stomata open at NIGHT, fixing CO₂ into organic acids, so gas exchange happens when it is cool and humid — decoupling CO₂ uptake from water loss. Spines: reduce leaf surface area (less transpiration) AND deter herbivores in a food-scarce habitat. Each adaptation maps to a distinct pressure.

questions.concept: Ecological succession — direction of the arrow
questions.question: Why does succession on bare rock move toward a more stable community, and what distinguishes the pioneer from the climax stage?
questions.solution: Each stage modifies the environment (lichens produce acid, weathering rock into soil; mosses deepen it; grasses, shrubs, trees follow) — the changes favour the NEXT stage more than the current one. Pioneers tolerate the harsh bare surface but build the conditions that replace them; the CLIMAX community is self-replacing and in equilibrium with the local climate. Succession is environment-building, not just species replacement.

questions.question: Why does energy flow one-way through an ecosystem while nutrients cycle? Give the thermodynamic reason.
questions.solution: Energy enters as sunlight, passes through trophic levels losing ~90% as heat at each transfer (second law), and LEAVES as unusable heat — it cannot be reused, so a constant input (the sun) is required. Nutrients are MATTER: they are conserved and recycled by decomposers back to producers. One-way flow vs closed cycling is the fundamental asymmetry of ecosystems.
